Creative Leadership in the Late Ottoman Era: The Work, Torah Teaching and National Influence of Rabbi Raphael Yehuda Menachem Levi (Yehuda Margoza)
This essay surveys the life and teaching of Rabbi Raphael Yehuda Menachem Levi (Yehuda Margoza), a key figure who shaped the renewal of the Jewish community of Jaffa in the nineteenth century. The text presents Margoza's transition from traditional Torah study to the adoption of an active conception of redemption, one that advocates a harmonious combination of spiritual life with agricultural labour and economic independence. Through a historical survey and chronological tables, it highlights his practical achievements, such as founding the Jewish community of Jaffa, planting the first Hebrew orchard and establishing public institutions that united Sephardim and Ashkenazim. Ultimately, the article seeks to illuminate the figure of Margoza as a pioneer who laid the foundations for modern religious Zionism and for the growth of the first Hebrew city.
Creative Leadership in the Late Ottoman Era: The Work, Torah Teaching and National Influence of Rabbi Raphael Yehuda Menachem Levi (Yehuda Margoza)
During the nineteenth century, profound changes took place in the demographic and economic structure of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel, changes that laid the practical and conceptual foundations for the growth of the Zionist movement and the building of the New Yishuv [cite: 1, 2]. At the heart of these pioneering processes stands the figure of Rabbi Raphael Yehuda Menachem Levi, known by his nickname "Rabbi Yehuda Margoza" [cite: 2]. As a spiritual leader, an agricultural entrepreneur and a public figure of many achievements, Margoza presented a unique model of leadership that sought to break down the walls of economic dependence of the Old Yishuv, through a well-founded theological combination of profound Torah study with active material endeavour, cultivation of the soil and communal integration [cite: 1, 2, 3]. This essay presents a comprehensive analysis of his life story, examines the foundations of his Torah-Zionist teaching, and analyzes his public and agricultural work, which changed the face of the city of Jaffa and laid the foundations for the growth of the modern Hebrew metropolis [cite: 2].
Personal Biography and Formative Milestones
Raphael Yehuda Menachem Levi was born in 1783 in the city of Sarajevo in Bosnia and Herzegovina, under the rule of the Ottoman Empire, where he acquired his early Torah education in a local yeshiva and worked as a teacher [cite: 2, 4]. In his youth he moved to the port city of Dubrovnik in Croatia, which was known by its Venetian name "Ragusa" [cite: 2, 5]. From this city, in which there was an ancient Jewish community, derives the nickname under which he is engraved in historical memory, "Yehuda Margoza" (Yehuda of Ragusa) [cite: 2, 5]. This nickname was not current among his contemporaries, who usually called him "Mercado," "the Chacham Yehuda HaLevi" or "R' Yehuda HaLevi"; it was coined in 1855 by the Austrian-Jewish poet and physician Dr. Ludwig August Frankl during his visit to the Land of Israel [cite: 2].
In 1801, when he was only 18, Margoza immigrated to the Land of Israel with his family and settled in Jerusalem [cite: 2, 4]. He devoted eighteen years to intensive study in the yeshivas of Jerusalem, was ordained as a rabbi and joined the local rabbinic establishment [cite: 2, 4]. During this period he married Rosa, and with her raised a family of four children [cite: 2]. His father, Menachem HaLevi, also immigrated to the Land; there are two historical opinions concerning his fate: one holds that he died in Jerusalem about a year after his immigration, while the other identifies him with a member of the rabbinic court in Jerusalem, Menachem HaLevi "a resident of Bosnia," who died in December 1838 and was buried on the Mount of Olives beside his wife Rivka [cite: 2].
In 1819 Margoza went out on behalf of the rabbis of Jerusalem as a shadar (an emissary of the rabbis) to Kushta (Constantinople, Istanbul), where he stayed for about six years [cite: 2]. This mission was a decisive conceptual crossroads in his life [cite: 2]. During his stay in Constantinople he met Rabbi Yehuda Bibas, one of the great thinkers of that period and the grandfather of the author of "Or ha-Chayim" [cite: 2]. Rabbi Bibas presented to him a revolutionary messianic conception, according to which redemption would not come about in a passive, miraculous manner, but demands concrete human action from below, including physical immigration to the Land of Israel, settlement and independent economic development [cite: 1, 2]. This encounter left a deep mark on Margoza and shaped his worldview, which from then on focused on combining the vision of redemption with practical, pioneering action [cite: 1, 2]. Margoza was a polymath of broad education who, alongside his Torah erudition, commanded six languages: Hebrew, Arabic, Serbian, French, Turkish and Ladino [cite: 2, 4].

The Enterprise of Renewing the Jewish Community of Jaffa, and His Public Leadership
In 1825 Margoza was appointed by the rabbis of Jerusalem to serve as their official representative in Jaffa [cite: 2, 4]. The original purpose of the appointment was to give assistance and a welcome to the elderly, the sick and the Jewish immigrants who arrived through the port of Jaffa on their way to the holy cities of the Land of Israel [cite: 2]. At that time there was no active Jewish community in Jaffa, and Margoza found himself living in the city in complete solitude [cite: 2]. On his arrival Margoza met Yeshayahu Matalon, a Jew who had immigrated in 1817 and engaged in trade and in the purchase of land, having obtained a firman from the authorities [cite: 9]. Matalon was the only Jew living in Jaffa at that time, and Margoza worked to persuade him to remain in the city and not to move his residence, thereby preventing the departure of the only Jewish presence in the place [cite: 9].
In 1829 a significant demographic turning point occurred [cite: 2]. A ship carrying Jewish immigrants from Morocco was wrecked near the shores of Acre [cite: 2]. The survivors were left without a roof over their heads, and Margoza persuaded twelve of them to join him and settle in Jaffa [cite: 2]. This group, made up of immigrants from the lands of the Maghreb, constituted the first human nucleus of the renewed community [cite: 1, 2]. Margoza worked tirelessly for the social and cultural integration of the immigrants, and later both Sephardi and Ashkenazi Jews joined the community [cite: 2]. In 1840 he received significant political and institutional backing when he was officially appointed Chief Rabbi of Jaffa by the Chacham Bashi of Jerusalem, Rabbi Chaim Avraham Gagin [cite: 2, 6]. This appointment stabilized the legal and religious standing of the community in the eyes of the Ottoman authorities and gave Margoza broad authority to rehabilitate the city after the severe epidemics that had struck it [cite: 2].
One of his most important strategic initiatives for consolidating the community was the establishment of the Jewish cemetery in Jaffa in 1834 [cite: 2, 4, 6]. Until that year the Jews of Jaffa had been forced to carry their dead on an arduous and dangerous journey to Jerusalem for burial [cite: 2]. The purchase of the land for the cemetery (located today on Yehuda Margoza Street in the Ajami neighbourhood) not only solved a difficult practical problem, but constituted a symbolic and legal act of the first order, attesting to an intention of permanent settlement that was independent and free of total dependence on the institutions of Jerusalem [cite: 2, 10].
In 1863 Margoza initiated a further organizational breakthrough: the establishment of the "Jaffa Town Committee" [cite: 2]. This was the first joint public committee in the Land of Israel that operated in a non-sectarian manner and united Sephardi and Ashkenazi Jews under one roof [cite: 2]. The committee's first and most prominent activity was the establishment of a branch of the "Kol Yisrael Chaverim" society (KIAH, the Alliance Israélite Universelle) in Jaffa, which led to the opening of a modern school for boys on 12 March 1868, under the presidency of Chaim Amzalag [cite: 2].
Margoza's standing extended beyond the boundaries of the Jewish community [cite: 2]. He was known as a man of kindness, humble and pleasant to all, and he enjoyed enormous respect from the Muslim and Christian population of the city, whose members used to honour him publicly and kiss his hands [cite: 2]. His diplomatic leadership was also demonstrated in 1871, when at the age of 90 he travelled to Alexandria in Egypt in order to persuade Baron de Menasce to support the funding of a modern Talmud Torah in Jaffa, a need that had become urgent because of the rapid demographic growth of the community [cite: 2]. During this journey Margoza was photographed in a local studio in Alexandria [cite: 2]. This reproduction photograph (a black-and-white silver print measuring 8.7 by 13.8 cm), which was donated in 1935 to the Avraham Schwadron portrait collection at the National Library by Moshe Ashulin of Tel Aviv, is the only visual record of his likeness that has survived [cite: 2, 8].
His Torah Teaching: The Harmony of the Sacred and the Profane
Rabbi Yehuda Margoza's Torah teaching places him among the earliest and most important forerunners of modern religious Zionism [cite: 2]. In contrast to the conservative conceptions of some of the rabbis of the Old Yishuv in Jerusalem, who saw agricultural labour and secular studies as a threat to the world of Torah, Margoza developed a harmonious outlook that advocates the combination of "the sacred and the profane" [cite: 1, 3]. He was a tremendous Torah scholar, great in Torah, who lived the sacred but did not fear the profane; he studied, investigated and was well versed in the needs of the time and the hour, out of the understanding that historical processes demand an adaptation of the practical tools in order to preserve the vitality of the community [cite: 1].
A theological analysis of his teaching reveals several basic principles that illuminate the depth of his thought:
The Doctrine of Active Redemption
Under the influence of his principal teacher, Rabbi Yehuda Bibas, Margoza believed that the process of national redemption requires human awakening and active endeavour [cite: 1, 2]. The messianic aspiration cannot be content with prayers and passive expectation of a miracle, but must find expression in the purchase of land, the building of cities and the planting of orchards in the Land of Israel [cite: 1, 2]. Redemption, in his view, grows out of earthly action, and working the land is an inseparable part of the spiritual tikkun (repair) of the people of Israel in its land [cite: 1]. This outlook also connected him conceptually with Rabbi Yehuda Alkalai, and the two are regarded as pioneers of religious political-Zionist thought [cite: 2].
Rejection of the Halukka Institution, and Productivization
Margoza firmly opposed the international system of donations and charity of the "Halukka" (distribution), in which he saw a factor that atrophies the spiritual and physical strength of the people [cite: 2]. He called on the Jews to earn their living by the labour of their hands [cite: 1, 2]. In his eyes, agricultural work in the Holy Land is a supreme religious commandment that sanctifies the Name and connects a person to his land directly, while creating economic independence that will allow a true flourishing of Torah not dependent on the favours of strangers [cite: 1].
Combining Torah with Derekh Eretz and General Education
Margoza himself served as a personal example of this conception [cite: 1]. He combined his Torah erudition with his command of many languages and a demonstrated deep understanding of economic management and external relations [cite: 2, 4]. This approach also guided him in his educational activity, when he supported the establishment of educational institutions that combined sacred studies with the acquisition of a trade, language and sciences, out of the understanding that a broad education is an essential tool for coping with the challenges of a changing reality [cite: 2].
The Agricultural Revolution in the Land of Israel: From the Orchard to Mikveh Israel
Rabbi Yehuda Margoza was not content with ideological moral preaching but worked to put his teaching into practice, and he was among the first Jewish farmers of the modern era in the Land of Israel [cite: 2]. In 1842, together with his colleagues the sages Avraham Penso and Yechiel Bechar, Margoza purchased an area of about 103 dunams on the banks of the Ayalon stream (Wadi Musrara), north-east of Jaffa [cite: 2, 4]. On this land the partners planted a spacious orchard containing more than 5,300 trees, of which about 2,200 were citrus trees [cite: 2]. This was the first modern orchard in the Land of Israel owned, managed and worked by Jews [cite: 2, 7].
In a historic letter that he wrote in 1853 to the British-Jewish philanthropist Moses Montefiore, Margoza tried to encourage him to purchase the orchard and to develop further agricultural initiatives in the Land [cite: 2, 7]. In this letter Margoza proudly stressed his primacy:
"I hereby declare that I am the first Israelite who came here to Jaffa and began, alone, to work the land by planting a garden" [cite: 7].
He undertook to do everything in his power to promote agricultural work among the seventy families that then made up his community [cite: 2]. In 1855 the orchard was indeed purchased by Montefiore and became the "Montefiore Orchard" (the area in which the Montefiore neighbourhood of Tel Aviv lies today) [cite: 2].
Margoza's involvement in agricultural development did not stop there [cite: 2]. In 1870, when Karl Netter worked to establish the agricultural school "Mikveh Israel," he met with fierce opposition from Haredi rabbinic circles in Jerusalem who feared secularization and a change in the traditional order of education [cite: 2]. Margoza, who saw this initiative as a clear realization of his Torah teaching combining the sacred and the profane, gave Netter full halakhic and public backing [cite: 1, 2]. He helped him acquire the institution's lands through his personal connections with the Chief Rabbi in Constantinople, and thereby made a decisive contribution to the success of the pioneering project [cite: 2]. A further strong testimony to his commitment to Hebrew agriculture was given in his last days when, lying on his deathbed, mortally ill, Margoza sent a warm and moving letter of blessing to the founders of the moshava of Petah Tikva ("the Mother of the Moshavot"), in which he blessed them on the establishment of the new agricultural settlement and wished them great success in their national enterprise [cite: 2].

His Death, Burial and Commemoration
Rabbi Raphael Yehuda Menachem Levi died on 6 August 1879 (17 Av 5639) at the advanced age of about 96, after more than half a century of undisputed spiritual and public leadership in Jaffa [cite: 2, 11]. His death aroused heavy and deep mourning throughout the country [cite: 11]. Thousands of people took part in his funeral procession, among them the rabbis of Jerusalem, foreign diplomats and consuls, Christian priests and Muslim sheikhs [cite: 11]. As a sign of mourning, all the merchants of Jaffa, Jews, Muslims and Christians alike, closed their businesses for three days, an extraordinary gesture that attested to his undisputed public standing and his position as a bridge between the various communities in the city [cite: 11].
Margoza was buried in the old Jewish cemetery of Jaffa, which he himself had founded in 1834 [cite: 2, 4]. Poetic words of appreciation were engraved on his tombstone, commemorating his standing, his wisdom and his leadership:
"The crown has been lifted, the righteous teacher who enlightened the eyes; the diadem has been taken away, the prince and counsellor, the elder and cunning artificer, a garland of grace, the man of rank and the eloquent orator; and mourning and lamentation have increased in the house of Yehuda" [cite: 12].
On another part of the tombstone the wording noting his long years of service was engraved:
"The all-embracing rabbi, our teacher and master Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi, ninety-six years old at his death, and for Da"N [54] years he judged Yafet"o [Jaffa, may it be speedily rebuilt and established], ve-hama"kh, on the To"V [17th] of the month of Menachem [Av], the year 5639 from the creation of the world; may his soul be bound up in the bond of life" [cite: 2].
Beside Rabbi Margoza, in the ancient cemetery in the Ajami neighbourhood, are buried many of the founders of the Jewish community of Jaffa and other prominent figures who accompanied the enterprise of settlement, among them Moshe Yaakov Blattner, Rabbi Moshe Elkayam, and his partner in agricultural endeavour, Yechiel Bechar [cite: 6]. This historic cemetery, located at 54 Rabbi Yehuda Margoza Street, has been restored and reopened to the public, and it constitutes living testimony to the beginnings of independent Jewish settlement outside the walls [cite: 10].
Rabbi Yehuda Margoza's legacy extends over several historical and conceptual dimensions:
Laying the foundations for the city of Tel Aviv: the small Jewish community that Margoza founded in Jaffa in 1825, absorbing immigrants from the lands of the Maghreb and merging them with immigrants from Europe, constituted the demographic, economic and cultural basis from which the Jewish neighbourhoods of Jaffa later developed, and out of them grew the first Hebrew city, Tel Aviv [cite: 1, 2].
Father of modern Hebrew agriculture: his work in the first Hebrew orchard and at Mikveh Israel paved the way for the transition of the Jews of the Land of Israel from a life of idleness and economic dependence to a life of creativity, productivity and physical connection to the soil, while rejecting the Halukka model and proving the ability of Jews to engage in modern and flourishing agriculture [cite: 1, 2, 7].
Forerunner of Zionism and a model of inter-communal unity: Margoza implemented a model of leadership that combined inter-communal and interreligious cooperation [cite: 2]. The establishment of the joint Jaffa Town Committee, which united Sephardim and Ashkenazim, constituted a historic precedent for breaking down the communal partitions in the Land of Israel, and proved that it is possible to conduct a united communal life under a shared national goal [cite: 2].
In recognition of his work and of his historic contribution to freeing the Yishuv from the shackles of economic atrophy, one of the main historic streets of Jaffa was named after him, Yehuda Margoza Street, which runs near the ancient Jewish cemetery that he established with his own hands [cite: 2, 10]. His figure remains engraved in the pages of history as a spiritual and practical father of the new Jewish settlement in the Land of Israel, and his deeds continue to be a source of inspiration for the connection between the values of tradition, the development of the Land and social unity [cite: 1, 2, 3].
